Subject: Sorry about the late section

Hi Imran,

I am sending my part of the report at 6 a.m., and I owe you an apology. On Monday I looked at the topic, thought "two hours, easy", and went to the cricket nets instead. On Wednesday I started the draft at ten at night. The tables took much longer than I guessed, the charts would not load, and I ended up working until dawn. This is not the first time. Every week I think two hours will do and every week it takes a whole night.

You had to wait for my section before you could join the pieces. I am sorry for that. Please tell me what you need corrected.

Mohit

qa.q: At what time did Mohit send the report section?
qa.a: Mohit sent the section at 6 a.m.

qa.q: What did Mohit think when first looking at the topic on Monday?
qa.a: Mohit thought it would take two hours and would be easy, which made it feel safe to postpone.

qa.q: What could Mohit try instead of guessing two hours, and why?
qa.a: Mohit could note how long the last two reports took and use that figure, because past times are a truer guide than a hopeful guess.

qa.q: How might Imran feel about waiting for the section?
qa.a: Imran may feel stressed and annoyed at having to wait, since the joining of the pieces could only begin after Mohit finished.

grounding: A student expects a report to take two hours, starts late and needs a whole night, repeating the same underestimate each week.

Uday, you asked why I'm always a zombie on Thursdays. Okay. It's Lalremsiami, and here's my weekly disaster, on repeat.
Every Monday we get a lab report due Thursday morning. Every Monday I think: two hours, easy. So I don't start on Monday. Or Tuesday. On Wednesday after dinner, I sit down at nine.
Then the graphs take an hour because the software is annoying. The analysis needs a formula I don't remember. I have to redo a table. At one, I'm halfway. At four, I'm writing the conclusion with my eyes closing. I submit at 8:55 and sleep through my ten o'clock class.
The funny part is, I've never once finished in two hours. Not once, this whole semester. Nine reports, nine all-nighters. And every Monday I still say 'two hours'.
So yes. Thursday zombie.

qa.q: What time is the report submitted?
How does Lalremsiami seem to feel about the pattern?
qa.a: Lalremsiami sounds tired and half amused, half frustrated, seeing the same underestimate repeat nine times.

qa.q: What would you change first in Lalremsiami's approach?
qa.a: Use the real past time, a whole night, as the estimate, and start on Monday or Tuesday evening instead of Wednesday.

qa.q: How might Uday see Lalremsiami on Thursdays?
qa.a: Uday sees a friend exhausted and missing class, and may feel concerned that the pattern keeps repeating.

grounding: Shows a student who keeps assuming a weekly report takes two hours, starts late, and spends every Wednesday night on it.

I'm Darshan, Jatin's roommate. Every Tuesday evening he says the same thing about his case-study write-up: 'Two hours, max. I'll do it after dinner tomorrow.'
Every Wednesday after dinner he opens the laptop at ten. By midnight he's still reading the case. At two he's making coffee, and at four the desk lamp is still on while I'm trying to sleep. On Thursday morning he submits just before the deadline, eyes red.
Last week I counted: seven weeks, seven all-nighters. I asked him once why he doesn't start on Monday. He said, 'It's only a two-hour job, it doesn't need a Monday.' He really seemed to believe it.
I can't tell what's going on in his head. But every Wednesday I put in earplugs, and every Thursday he says, 'Next week will be quicker.'

qa.q: How many all-nighters did Darshan count?
What does Jatin's 'It's only a two-hour job' suggest about his thinking?
qa.a: It suggests he feels overconfident and stuck in the same hopeful estimate, not letting past weeks change his plan.

qa.q: What could Jatin try next week?
qa.a: Look back at how long the last seven took, plan for that, and start on Monday with a first hour of reading.

qa.q: What is it like for Darshan every Wednesday?
qa.a: Darshan loses sleep to the desk lamp and has to use earplugs, watching the same pattern repeat.

grounding: Shows a student who keeps thinking a write-up takes two hours, starts late and stays up all night, repeating the same underestimate every week.
